title: Cloudflare launches Search for Agents: one toggle that lets AI agents search your site directly
summary: Site owners no longer need to build a retrieval backend by hand: flip a toggle in the Cloudflare dashboard, and your site gets indexed automatically and exposes a search endpoint under your own domain that AI agents can discover on their own.
ai_summary: Cloudflare has released Search for Agents: website search that used to require manual setup and integration is now a dashboard toggle. Turn it on and Cloudflare automatically creates an AI Search instance for your domain, crawls and indexes its content, and injects metadata on every page so any AI agent can discover and call the /.well-known/search endpoint on your own domain. Search results come back as Markdown, not answers generated by another model, so agents can use them directly as raw material. It also natively supports the new HTTP QUERY method, which became RFC 10008 in June 2026. The feature is open to all customers, including the Free plan with limits; usage follows AI Search pricing. The biggest gap is that Cloudflare hasn't published the Free tier's specific quota.
brief: Flip one toggle and Cloudflare automatically creates an AI Search instance, crawls and indexes your site.
Metadata is injected into every page, so agents discover the /.well-known/search endpoint and reuse it on their own.
What comes back is retrieved Markdown content, not an AI-generated answer.
It natively supports the RFC 10008 HTTP QUERY method; the Free plan is available with limits.

blocks.p: Cloudflare already had a service called AI Search that indexes your content and lets you add search to any app or agent without building your own retrieval backend. It has also supported using your website as a data source for a while, automatically crawling pages and turning them into an index.

The catch is that enabling AI Search for a website still meant manual work: you had to create and configure an instance, then do the integration to put the search endpoint on your own domain and make sure agents knew where to find the index and how to use it.

Search for Agents collapses all of that into one toggle. Turn it on for a zone in the dashboard, and Cloudflare automatically creates the AI Search instance, starts indexing your content, and makes search discoverable and callable from your own domain.

sections.h: What happens behind the scenes when you flip the toggle?

blocks.p: The toggle lives under Quick Actions on your zone page in the dashboard, and you can also enable it via the API. Once it's on, Cloudflare automatically creates an AI Search instance and starts crawling and indexing the content in that zone; the developer docs explain how the crawl works.

The instance starts with default settings, and you can turn on reranking or change options like cache settings whenever you like. Because it's still an AI Search instance underneath, all the standard features are there: a public REST API, MCP endpoints, access from Workers, or an embedded search box for human visitors.
Who can search, and whether they can, still depends on your domain's existing settings, such as bot management, AI Crawl Control, and WAF rules.

sections.h: How do agents know your site is searchable?

blocks.p: Having an endpoint isn't enough; agents first need to know it exists. Search for Agents advertises it on every page of your site.

For HTML responses, it injects a set of meta tags into the page's <head>: agent:instructions tells agents to use the search endpoint instead of crawling page by page, agent:endpoint gives the endpoint address, agent:method says GET, and agent:documentation points to the docs.
If you also have Markdown for Agents enabled, agents that request a page with Accept: text/markdown get the same information, just placed in YAML front matter.

sections.h: What does search return? How is that different from having AI answer directly?

blocks.p: Once an agent finds the endpoint, it can call it directly. A plain GET request, such as a search for "cloudflare artifacts", returns relevant pages whose content has already been converted to Markdown, ranked by relevance — in the example, the first result scores 1.000 and the second 0.951.

Depending on your AI Search configuration, an agent can also ask in natural language, such as "What is the maximum push size for Cloudflare Artifacts?", and the endpoint returns relevant documentation snippets.

The key difference is what comes back: the endpoint returns retrieved content, not a generated answer. The agent already has a model and conversation context, so it only needs raw information from your site — not another model answering on your behalf.

fig.title: The endpoint supports GET and the new QUERY method
fig.subtitle: Call examples from Cloudflare's blog
fig.note: The first example is a plain GET; the next two use the new HTTP QUERY method with plain-text and JSON request bodies
fig.code:
curl "https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search?q=cloudflare+artifacts"

curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --data 'What is the maximum payload size per ingestion request in Basin Pipelines?'

curl -X QUERY 'https://developers.cloudflare.com/.well-known/search' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"q":"How many bulk import requests per minute does Email Service allow?"}'

sections.h: What's the new HTTP QUERY method?

blocks.p: Beyond a normal GET, Search for Agents natively supports the new HTTP QUERY method. QUERY is an IETF Proposed Standard, published as RFC 10008 in June 2026, and Cloudflare's James Snell is one of its co-authors.
It lets a client put search criteria in the request body and send them safely and idempotently, without changing server state — a good fit for AI search's ask-without-changing pattern.

Adoption is still underway: major browser vendors are discussing the RFC, and clients and frameworks such as curl and undici have adopted it or are considering it. Search for Agents accepts either a plain-text or JSON request body.
Starting today, Search for Agents is available to all customers, including the Free plan, but the announcement only says it comes with limits.
Usage follows AI Search pricing: ingesting content, storing index content, and serving queries are all billed, subject to the included usage and limits on the Workers Free and Paid plans.
In other words, Free users can get started, but the announcement doesn't publish the Free tier's specific quotas.

list: The Free plan's specific limits — how many pages it can index, or how many queries it can serve per month — aren't specified.
How often the index refreshes, or how quickly new pages become searchable, is only answered with "see the developer docs."
No comparison is provided against similar site-search-for-agents offerings on results quality or pricing.
There's no specific timeline for QUERY adoption across browsers and frameworks.
The specific rules for whether the feature's own AI crawler traffic is handled under AI Crawl Control aren't given; Cloudflare only says it's subject to your domain settings.

blocks.p: The value is less work: if you run a content or docs site and want agents like OpenAI or OpenCode to be able to look up your material when answering, you don't have to write code or run a retrieval service, and the endpoint stays on your own domain.

The trade-offs are clear too: Cloudflare will crawl and index your content, usage is billed under AI Search pricing, and the Free plan has limits. What can actually be searched also depends on your WAF, bot management, and AI Crawl Control settings.

list: If you have a docs or content site and want AI tools to be able to find your pages, this toggle is the lowest-effort starting point.
If you already use Cloudflare and don't want to build a retrieval backend, try it right from Quick Actions.
If you're wary about exposing content to agents, check the Agent Readiness page and AI Crawl Control first, then decide whether to enable it.

sources.note: All facts come from Cloudflare's official blog; the flow diagrams are illustrative, and the code and metadata examples are from the blog post. The Free tier's specific quota is not stated.
